subproblems.title: Cut-off quadratic moments over n-planes (reused accepted theorem)
subproblems.statement: For every natural number n ≥ 1 there is a real constant c > 0, depending only on n, such that for every P ∈ ℕ, every linear subspace Q ⊆ ℝ^P with dim Q = n and every u ∈ ℝ^P: ∫_Q max(1 − |y|², 0)⟨u, y⟩² dHⁿ(y) = c·|p_Q u|². Here Hⁿ = μHE[n] is the normalized n-dimensional Hausdorff measure on ℝ^P, ∫_Q is the Bochner integral against Hⁿ⌞Q, ⟨·,·⟩ is the Euclidean inner product, and p_Q = Q.starProjection is the orthogonal projection onto Q.
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ n : ℕ, 0 < n → ∃ c : ℝ, 0 < c ∧ ∀ (P : ℕ) (Q : Submodule ℝ (Euclid P)), Module.finrank ℝ Q = n → ∀ u : Euclid P, ∫ y in (Q : Set (Euclid P)), max (1 - ‖y‖ ^ 2) 0 * inner ℝ u y ^ 2 ∂μHE[n] = c * ‖Q.starProjection u‖ ^ 2
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source: step 5 of the parent proof, which computes ∫_Q f_u dHⁿ = c_n|p_Q u|². There f_u(y) = χ(|y|²)⟨u, y⟩², χ(t) = max(1 − t, 0), and c_n := ∫_{ℝⁿ} χ(|z|²) z₁² dz. The same computation is the comparator-accepted DAG node root.half_space_cone_lies_in_boundary-a1.tangent_projection_aemeasurable-a1.plane_quadratic_moment-a1. Its declaration Submission.exists_plane_cutoff_quadratic_moment_eq has exactly this frozen type and is reused here. Step 5 is written out below with all details.

Notation.
- Fix n ≥ 1.
- E_n := ℝⁿ = EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin n), with Lebesgue measure Lⁿ. On E_n, Hⁿ = Lⁿ (EuclideanSpace.euclideanHausdorffMeasure_eq_volume).
- Since n ≥ 1, the index i₀ := 0 ∈ Fin n exists.
- For i, j ∈ Fin n put h_{ij}(z) := max(1 − |z|², 0)·z_i·z_j.
- c := ∫_{E_n} h_{i₀i₀} dLⁿ. Only n enters this definition. It does not depend on P, Q or u.

1. Integrability.
- Each h_{ij} is continuous: it is built from the norm, the coordinate maps, max and products.
- If |z| > 1, then 1 − |z|² < 0, so max(1 − |z|², 0) = 0 and h_{ij}(z) = 0.
- So h_{ij} has support in the closed unit ball, which is compact.
- Lⁿ is finite on compact sets, so each h_{ij} is Lⁿ-integrable (Continuous.integrable_of_hasCompactSupport).

2. Off-diagonal moments vanish. Let i ≠ j, and let S : E_n → E_n negate the i-th coordinate.
- S is a linear isometry equivalence, so |Sz| = |z|.
- S preserves Lⁿ (LinearIsometryEquiv.measurePreserving).
- S is a homeomorphism, hence a measurable embedding.
- Since (Sz)_i = −z_i and (Sz)_j = z_j, h_{ij}(Sz) = −h_{ij}(z) for all z.
- By change of variables (MeasurePreserving.integral_comp), ∫ h_{ij} dLⁿ = ∫ h_{ij}(Sz) dLⁿ(z) = −∫ h_{ij} dLⁿ.
- Hence ∫ h_{ij} dLⁿ = 0.

3. Every diagonal moment equals c. Fix i, and let T : E_n → E_n swap the coordinates i₀ and i.
- T is a linear isometry equivalence. It preserves Lⁿ, |Tz| = |z| and (Tz)_i = z_{i₀}.
- Hence h_{ii}(Tz) = max(1 − |z|², 0)z_{i₀}² = h_{i₀i₀}(z).
- By change of variables, ∫ h_{ii} dLⁿ = ∫ h_{ii}(Tz) dLⁿ(z) = ∫ h_{i₀i₀} dLⁿ = c.

4. 0 < c < ∞.
- Finiteness is step 1.
- h_{i₀i₀} is continuous, ≥ 0 and compactly supported.
- At z* := ½e_{i₀} we have |z*|² = 1/4, so h_{i₀i₀}(z*) = (3/4)(1/4) = 3/16 ≠ 0.
- Lⁿ is positive on nonempty open sets and finite on compact sets. So the integral is > 0 (Continuous.integral_pos_of_hasCompactSupport_nonneg_nonzero).
- The constant c is now fixed. Everything below uses this same c.

5. Parametrizing Q.
- Let P ∈ ℕ, a subspace Q ⊆ ℝ^P with dim Q = n, and u ∈ ℝ^P be arbitrary. If n > P there is no such Q, and nothing is to be proved.
- Choose an orthonormal basis τ₁, …, τ_n of Q, and put ι(z) := Σ_i z_iτ_i.
- By orthonormality, ι : E_n → ℝ^P is a linear isometry (|ιz| = |z|).
- The range of ι is exactly Q: every q ∈ Q is ι of its coordinate vector, and every Σ z_iτ_i lies in Q.

6. Push-forward of Hausdorff measure.
- Since ι is an isometry, the push-forward of Hⁿ on E_n under ι is Hⁿ⌞range ι = Hⁿ⌞Q (Isometry.map_euclideanHausdorffMeasure).
- An isometry from a complete space is a closed embedding, hence a measurable embedding.
- Put F(y) := max(1 − |y|², 0)⟨u, y⟩². Then ∫_Q F dHⁿ = ∫_{E_n} F(ιz) dHⁿ(z) = ∫_{E_n} F(ιz) dLⁿ(z) (MeasurableEmbedding.integral_map, then Hⁿ = Lⁿ on E_n).

7. Expanding the integrand.
- Let a_i := ⟨u, τ_i⟩.
- Then |ιz| = |z| and ⟨u, ιz⟩ = Σ_i a_iz_i.
- So F(ιz) = max(1 − |z|², 0)(Σ_i a_iz_i)² = Σ_iΣ_j a_ia_j h_{ij}(z).

8. Integrating.
- The finitely many functions a_ia_jh_{ij} are integrable (step 1), so the integral is additive and homogeneous.
- So ∫_{E_n} F(ιz) dLⁿ = Σ_{i,j} a_ia_j ∫ h_{ij} dLⁿ.
- By steps 2 and 3, only the terms with j = i survive, and each equals a_i²c.
- Hence ∫_Q F dHⁿ = c·Σ_i a_i².

9. Identifying Σ_i a_i².
- p_Q u = Σ_i ⟨τ_i, u⟩τ_i, the expansion in an orthonormal basis of Q.
- By orthonormality, |p_Q u|² = Σ_i ⟨τ_i, u⟩² = Σ_i a_i².

10. Conclusion.
- By steps 6–9, ∫_Q max(1 − |y|², 0)⟨u, y⟩² dHⁿ(y) = c|p_Q u|².
- c > 0 was fixed in step 4, before P, Q and u were chosen in step 5. So one c works for every P, every n-dimensional Q ⊆ ℝ^P and every u. ∎
proof_key_steps: Define c := ∫_{ℝⁿ} max(1−|z|²,0) z_{i₀}² dLⁿ, which depends only on n. Each h_{ij}(z) = max(1−|z|²,0)z_iz_j is continuous with support in the closed unit ball, hence integrable.
Coordinate reflections, which are measure-preserving linear isometries, give ∫h_{ij} = 0 for i ≠ j. Coordinate swaps give ∫h_{ii} = c.
c > 0: the integrand is continuous, ≥ 0, compactly supported and equals 3/16 at e_{i₀}/2.
An orthonormal basis of Q gives a linear isometry ι : ℝⁿ → ℝ^P onto Q with ι_#Hⁿ = Hⁿ⌞Q. So ∫_Q F dHⁿ = ∫ F∘ι dLⁿ.
F∘ι = Σ a_ia_jh_{ij} with a_i = ⟨u,τ_i⟩, so the integral is cΣa_i² = c|p_Q u|², with the same c for every P, Q and u.

subproblems.title: A field of orthogonal projections is a.e.-measurable when its quadratic forms are (reused accepted theorem)
subproblems.statement: Let P ∈ ℕ, let μ be any measure on ℝ^P with its Borel σ-algebra, and let K : ℝ^P → {linear subspaces of ℝ^P} be any map. Write p_x := (K x).starProjection for the orthogonal projection onto K(x), an element of the space L(ℝ^P, ℝ^P) of continuous linear maps with its operator-norm topology and Borel σ-algebra. Suppose that for every u ∈ ℝ^P the real function x ↦ |p_x u|² is μ-a.e. measurable. Then x ↦ p_x is μ-a.e. measurable (AEMeasurable).
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (P : ℕ) (μ : Measure (Euclid P)) (K : Euclid P → Submodule ℝ (Euclid P)), (∀ u : Euclid P, AEMeasurable (fun x => ‖(K x).starProjection u‖ ^ 2) μ) → AEMeasurable (fun x => (K x).starProjection) μ
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source: steps 8 and 9 of the parent proof (polarization and assembly). They use only that each p_x is an orthogonal projection, so they are stated here for an arbitrary measure μ and an arbitrary field K of subspaces. This is the comparator-accepted DAG node root.half_space_cone_lies_in_boundary-a1.tangent_projection_aemeasurable-a1.projection_field_aemeasurable-a1. Its declaration Submission.aemeasurable_starProjection_of_aemeasurable_norm_sq has exactly this frozen type and is reused here.

Notation.
- ⟨·,·⟩ is the Euclidean inner product of ℝ^P, and p_x := (K x).starProjection.
- L(ℝ^P, ℝ^P) carries the operator-norm topology and its Borel σ-algebra (ContinuousLinearMap.instMeasurableSpace = borel).

1. Self-adjointness and idempotence.
- For every x and all v, w ∈ ℝ^P, ⟨p_x v, w⟩ = ⟨v, p_x w⟩ (Submodule.inner_starProjection_left_eq_right).
- p_x(p_x w) = p_x w, because p_x w ∈ K(x) and p_x fixes K(x) pointwise.

2. Polarization. Let u, w ∈ ℝ^P.
- By step 1, ⟨p_x u, w⟩ = ⟨u, p_x w⟩ = ⟨u, p_x(p_x w)⟩ = ⟨p_x u, p_x w⟩.
- For real vectors a, b, |a ± b|² = |a|² ± 2⟨a, b⟩ + |b|², so ⟨a, b⟩ = (|a + b|² − |a − b|²)/4.
- Take a = p_x u and b = p_x w, and use p_x u ± p_x w = p_x(u ± w).
- This gives, for every x: ⟨p_x u, w⟩ = (|p_x(u + w)|² − |p_x(u − w)|²)/4.

3. The coefficients are a.e. measurable.
- By hypothesis, applied to the vectors u + w and u − w, x ↦ |p_x(u + w)|² and x ↦ |p_x(u − w)|² are μ-AEMeasurable.
- Differences and constant multiples of AEMeasurable real functions are AEMeasurable.
- So by step 2, x ↦ ⟨p_x u, w⟩ is μ-AEMeasurable for all u, w ∈ ℝ^P.

4. Basis expansion. Let e_1, …, e_P be the standard orthonormal basis of ℝ^P.
- For (a, b) ∈ Fin P × Fin P, let L_{ab} ∈ L(ℝ^P, ℝ^P), L_{ab}(v) := ⟨e_a, v⟩e_b.
- Let Λ : ℝ^{Fin P × Fin P} → L(ℝ^P, ℝ^P), Λ(m) := Σ_{a,b} m_{ab}L_{ab}.
- Put g(x) := (⟨p_x e_a, e_b⟩)_{(a,b)}.
- Fix x and v. Since v = Σ_a ⟨e_a, v⟩e_a, p_x v = Σ_a ⟨e_a, v⟩p_x e_a.
- Also p_x e_a = Σ_b ⟨p_x e_a, e_b⟩e_b.
- So p_x v = Σ_{a,b} ⟨p_x e_a, e_b⟩⟨e_a, v⟩e_b = Λ(g(x))(v). Hence p_x = Λ(g(x)) for every x.

5. Conclusion.
- Λ is a finite sum of the continuous linear maps m ↦ m_{ab}L_{ab}, so it is continuous linear, hence Borel measurable.
- g is μ-AEMeasurable as a map into the finite product ℝ^{Fin P × Fin P}, because each coordinate is (step 3; AEMeasurable.of_eval).
- A measurable map composed with a μ-AEMeasurable map is μ-AEMeasurable (Measurable.comp_aemeasurable). So x ↦ p_x = Λ(g(x)) is μ-AEMeasurable.
- If P = 0, all spaces are trivial and the same argument applies with empty sums. ∎
proof_key_steps: Each p_x is self-adjoint and idempotent, so ⟨p_x u, w⟩ = ⟨p_x u, p_x w⟩ = (|p_x(u+w)|² − |p_x(u−w)|²)/4.
Hence every matrix coefficient x ↦ ⟨p_x e_a, e_b⟩ is μ-a.e. measurable.
p_x = Λ((⟨p_x e_a, e_b⟩)_{a,b}), where Λ(m) = Σ m_{ab}⟨e_a,·⟩e_b is a continuous linear map on the finite-dimensional coefficient space.
A continuous map composed with an a.e.-measurable map into ℝ^{P×P} is a.e.-measurable.

subproblems.title: The carrier measure of an integer multiplicity triple in an open set is σ-finite
subproblems.statement: Let P, n ∈ ℕ, let U ⊆ ℝ^P be open, and let R = (M, θ, ξ) be an IMRep U n. That is: M = R.carrier is a Borel, countably n-rectifiable subset of U; θ = R.mult : ℝ^P → ℕ is measurable, with θ(x) > 0 (so θ(x) ≥ 1) for x ∈ M and ∫_{M∩K} θ dHⁿ < ∞ for every compact K ⊆ U; and ξ = R.orient is Hⁿ⌞M-a.e. strongly measurable and, Hⁿ⌞M-a.e., orients an approximate tangent plane of M. Then ν := Hⁿ⌞M (μHE[n].restrict R.carrier) is a σ-finite measure.
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (P n : ℕ) (U : Set (Euclid P)) (R : IMRep U n), IsOpen U → SigmaFinite (μHE[n].restrict R.carrier)
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source: step 2, parts (a)–(d), of the parent proof. The parent needs this σ-finiteness for Tonelli's theorem in step 6. The proof uses only four fields of R: M ⊆ U (R.carrier_subset), M Borel (R.measurableSet_carrier), θ > 0 on M (R.mult_pos) and the local integrability of θ (R.locallyIntegrable_mult). Notation: Hⁿ := μHE[n] and ν := Hⁿ⌞M.

1. Compact exhaustion of U. There are compact sets K_0, K_1, K_2, … ⊆ U with ⋃_j K_j = U.
- If U = ℝ^P, take K_j := closedBall(0, j).
- Otherwise F := ℝ^P ∖ U is closed and nonempty, and d(y) := dist(y, F) = inf_{z∈F}|y − z| is 1-Lipschitz, hence continuous.
  - If y ∈ F, then d(y) = 0.
  - If y ∈ U, then, since U is open, some ball B(y, ε) ⊆ U misses F, so d(y) ≥ ε > 0.
  - Put K_j := {y : |y| ≤ j and d(y) ≥ 1/(j+1)}.
  - K_j is closed, as an intersection of preimages of closed sets under continuous maps, and bounded, hence compact (Heine–Borel).
  - K_j ⊆ {d > 0} = U.
  - For y ∈ U, choose j ≥ |y| with 1/(j+1) ≤ d(y), which is possible since d(y) > 0. Then y ∈ K_j. So ⋃_j K_j = U.
- Equivalent route used in Lean: U is an open subset of the locally compact, second-countable space ℝ^P. So U with the subspace topology is locally compact and second countable, hence σ-compact (IsOpen.locallyCompactSpace, sigmaCompactSpace_of_locallyCompact_secondCountable, isSigmaCompact_iff_sigmaCompactSpace).

2. Pieces of finite measure.
- Put B_j := M ∩ K_j. It is Borel: M is Borel, and K_j is compact, hence closed.
- For x ∈ B_j we have x ∈ M, so θ(x) ≥ 1, because θ is ℕ-valued and positive on M.
- Therefore Hⁿ(B_j) = ∫⁻_{B_j} 1 dHⁿ ≤ ∫⁻_{B_j} θ dHⁿ = ∫⁻_{M∩K_j} θ dHⁿ < ∞.
- The last bound is R.locallyIntegrable_mult, which applies because K_j is compact and K_j ⊆ U.

3. Covering.
- By R.carrier_subset and step 1, M ⊆ U = ⋃_j K_j, so M = ⋃_j B_j.
- Since B_j ⊆ M, ν(B_j) = Hⁿ(B_j ∩ M) = Hⁿ(B_j) < ∞.
- The Borel set C := ℝ^P ∖ M satisfies ν(C) = Hⁿ(C ∩ M) = Hⁿ(∅) = 0.

4. Conclusion.
- The Borel sets S_j := B_j ∪ C (j ∈ ℕ) satisfy ν(S_j) ≤ ν(B_j) + ν(C) < ∞.
- ⋃_j S_j = M ∪ C = ℝ^P.
- So ℝ^P is a countable union of Borel sets of finite ν-measure, and ν is σ-finite.
- In Lean one may instead apply SimonGMT's Poincare.SimonGMT.Chapter03.sigmaFinite_restrict_of_hausdorff_finite_cover to the cover M ⊆ ⋃_j B_j with Hⁿ(B_j) < ∞. ∎
proof_key_steps: The open set U is a countable union of compact sets K_j ⊆ U.
θ ≥ 1 on M and R.locallyIntegrable_mult give Hⁿ(M ∩ K_j) ≤ ∫⁻_{M∩K_j} θ dHⁿ < ∞.
M ⊆ U = ⋃K_j, so the Borel sets (M ∩ K_j) ∪ (ℝ^P ∖ M) have finite ν-measure and cover ℝ^P. Hence ν = Hⁿ⌞M is σ-finite.

subproblems.title: Borel measurability of the blow-up integrals in the definition of approximate tangent planes
subproblems.statement: Let P, n ∈ ℕ, and let M ⊆ ℝ^P be any set such that ν := Hⁿ⌞M (μHE[n].restrict M) is s-finite. Let f : ℝ^P → ℝ be continuous with f(y) ≥ 0 for all y, and let r > 0. For x ∈ ℝ^P let η_x(y) := r⁻¹(y − x) (SimonGMT blowUpMap x r). Then the real function x ↦ ∫_{η_x(M)} f dHⁿ is Borel measurable on ℝ^P. This is the Bochner integral of f against Hⁿ⌞η_x(M), the integral in Simon's Definition 1.4 of approximate tangent planes, and it is 0 when f is not integrable there.
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (P n : ℕ) (M : Set (Euclid P)), SFinite (μHE[n].restrict M) → ∀ f : Euclid P → ℝ, Continuous f → (∀ y, 0 ≤ f y) → ∀ r : ℝ, 0 < r → Measurable (fun x : Euclid P => ∫ y in Poincare.SimonGMT.Chapter03.blowUpMap x r '' M, f y ∂μHE[n])
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source: step 6, parts (a)–(d), of the parent proof. Here it is stated for an arbitrary set M with s-finite Hⁿ⌞M, a continuous f ≥ 0 and a fixed r > 0. In the parent, s-finiteness comes from step 2 and f is the test function f_u of step 4.

Notation.
- Hⁿ := μHE[n]. It is defined on every subset of ℝ^P (outer measure).
- ν := Hⁿ⌞M, s-finite by hypothesis.
- η_x(y) := r⁻¹(y − x) = blowUpMap x r y.
- c := r^{−n} = |r⁻¹|ⁿ.
- No measurability of M is assumed or needed.

1. Regularity of η.
- For fixed x, η_x is the translation y ↦ y − x followed by multiplication by r⁻¹. It is continuous, hence Borel measurable.
- The map (x, y) ↦ η_x(y) = r⁻¹(y − x) is continuous on ℝ^P × ℝ^P.

2. Scaling. For every x and every set s ⊆ ℝ^P, measurable or not, Hⁿ(η_x(s)) = c·Hⁿ(s).
- η_x(s) = r⁻¹·(s − x).
- The translation y ↦ y − x is an isometry, so Hⁿ(s − x) = Hⁿ(s) (Isometry.euclideanHausdorffMeasure_image).
- Since r⁻¹ ≠ 0, Hⁿ(r⁻¹·A) = |r⁻¹|ⁿHⁿ(A) for every set A (Measure.euclideanHausdorffMeasure_smul₀).

3. The restricted measure. For every x, Hⁿ⌞η_x(M) = c·(η_x)_#ν.
- Let B be Borel. Then η_x⁻¹(B) is Borel by step 1.
- η_x(M) ∩ B = η_x(M ∩ η_x⁻¹(B)); this holds for any map (image_inter_preimage).
- Using the restriction formula (Hⁿ⌞S)(T) = Hⁿ(T ∩ S) for Borel T, and step 2:
  (Hⁿ⌞η_x(M))(B) = Hⁿ(B ∩ η_x(M)) = Hⁿ(η_x(M ∩ η_x⁻¹(B))) = c·Hⁿ(η_x⁻¹(B) ∩ M) = c·ν(η_x⁻¹(B)) = c·((η_x)_#ν)(B).
- Measures that agree on all Borel sets are equal.

4. From the Bochner integral to a lower integral. Fix x.
- f ≥ 0 everywhere, and f is continuous, hence a.e. strongly measurable for every measure.
- So ∫_{η_x(M)} f dHⁿ = (∫⁻_{η_x(M)} ofReal(f) dHⁿ).toReal (integral_eq_lintegral_of_nonneg_ae).
- This holds whether or not f is integrable on η_x(M). If it is not, the lower integral is ∞ and ∞.toReal = 0, which is also the value of the Bochner integral.

5. Change of variables.
- By step 3, ∫⁻_{η_x(M)} ofReal(f) dHⁿ = c·∫⁻ ofReal(f) d((η_x)_#ν) (lintegral_smul_measure).
- This equals c·∫⁻ ofReal(f(η_x(y))) dν(y) (lintegral_map; ofReal∘f and η_x are measurable).

6. Tonelli.
- G(x, y) := ofReal(f(r⁻¹(y − x))) is a continuous map ℝ^P × ℝ^P → [0, ∞], by step 1 and the continuity of f and ofReal. So it is Borel measurable.
- ℝ^P is second countable, so the Borel σ-algebra of ℝ^P × ℝ^P is the product σ-algebra, and G is measurable for the product σ-algebra.
- Since ν is s-finite, x ↦ ∫⁻ G(x, y) dν(y) is measurable (Measurable.lintegral_prod_right').

7. Conclusion.
- By steps 4 and 5, ∫_{η_x(M)} f dHⁿ = (c·∫⁻ G(x, y) dν(y)).toReal for every x.
- Multiplication by the constant c and ENNReal.toReal preserve measurability.
- So x ↦ ∫_{η_x(M)} f dHⁿ is Borel measurable. ∎
proof_key_steps: Hⁿ(η_x(s)) = r^{−n}Hⁿ(s) for every set s: a translation isometry followed by the dilation r⁻¹.
Hence Hⁿ⌞η_x(M) = r^{−n}(η_x)_#(Hⁿ⌞M), checked on Borel sets via η_x(M) ∩ B = η_x(M ∩ η_x⁻¹B).
For f ≥ 0 continuous, ∫_{η_x(M)} f dHⁿ = (r^{−n}∫⁻ ofReal(f(r⁻¹(y−x))) dν(y)).toReal, even when f is not integrable there.
(x, y) ↦ ofReal(f(r⁻¹(y−x))) is continuous, hence product-measurable. Since ν is s-finite, Tonelli (Measurable.lintegral_prod_right') makes the x-integral measurable, and so is its toReal.
